You see, back then, we didn't have all these fancy credit cards and loans like they do now. We had to save our money and make do with what we had. And you know what? We thrived. We had to be frugal, but we were happy with what we had. (smiling) I remember my mother making clothes for my sister and me from flour sacks and scraps of fabric. We didn't need all these fancy clothes like they do now.

And during the war, we all pitched in. We had victory gardens, scrap metal drives, and we rationed food and gasoline. We didn't have all these entitlements like they do now. We worked hard and we were proud of it. (pausing, looking down) I think that's something that's been lost on younger folks. They don't know what it's like to have to struggle and make do.

I think that's something that's been lost in today's world. (shaking head) Kids these days, they're so focused on their own individuality and their own problems. They don't know what it's like to be part of a community. (sighing) Ah, well, that's just my opinion.
